findings.target: plan-v7 R2 test_strategy — TestABodyThatDoesNotMatchThePresignedDigestIsRefusedByTheBucket, and its twin TestABodyLongerThanTheSignedLength
findings.finding: The leg the whole step exists for cannot see the checksum. The plan's verbatim test code builds the PUT with `http.NewRequestWithContext(...)` and sets NO headers — but a URL from `PresignHeader` requires the client to replay every signed header byte-for-byte. Measured: with `x-amz-checksum-sha256` signed and the header omitted, MinIO answers 400 `AccessDenied` ("There were headers present in the request which were not signed") for LYING bytes AND for HONEST bytes alike. The leg's only assertion is `resp.StatusCode < 400`, so it is GREEN with zero digest verification happening anywhere. Four distinct failure modes all land in that status class and only the last is the control: AccessDenied (header not replayed), InvalidArgument (wrong encoding — see the hex finding), SignatureDoesNotMatch (wrong signed-header set), XAmzContentChecksumMismatch (the actual thing). The plan's stated intermediate red still works — `PresignedPutObject` + lying bytes really does return 200 — so the mutation proof passes while the green state proves only 'some signed header is required'.
findings.evidence: MinIO RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z, bucket lens-media, 29-byte body. P2-09, the plan's code verbatim: `PUT (no header replayed), LYING bytes -> 400 AccessDenied`; `PUT (no header replayed), HONEST bytes -> 400 AccessDenied`; `StatObject -> ABSENT`. Contrast P1-EXP-02, header replayed, lying bytes: `400 XAmzContentChecksumMismatch`, message "The provided 'x-amz-checksum' header does not match what was computed". Contrast P1-EXP-01, PresignedPutObject, lying bytes: `200`, object stored (confirmed by admin-credential StatObject, not by a HEAD).
findings.fix: Replay the header in the leg — `req.Header.Set("x-amz-checksum-sha256", base64Digest)` — and assert the S3 error CODE `XAmzContentChecksumMismatch` parsed out of the XML, not a status class. Add a positive-control leg in the same function: honest bytes + the same header -> 200 and the object present with the expected size. Without both halves the leg is satisfied by a server that refuses everything.

findings.target: plan-v7 R3 work item 1 (POST /v1/media response shape); docs/CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md
findings.finding: The begin response is `{id, uploadUrl, expiresAt, alreadyExists}` and carries no headers. A presigned PUT whose signature covers `x-amz-checksum-sha256` is unusable unless the caller sends that exact header with that exact value — and the value is the BASE64 digest while `id` and the wire format are HEX. A Flutter client handed only `uploadUrl` gets a 400 on every upload, forever, and has no way to derive the required header from the response without knowing the base64/hex convention. This is the direct consequence of DEC-43's own warning arriving one layer higher than expected: the seam is correct, the contract across it is missing.
findings.evidence: Header omitted -> `400 AccessDenied`, object absent. Header present with the wrong value -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`. Header present, correct -> `200`, and `StatObject{Checksum:true}` returns `sha256="o+vraIbU4qF4i74j6oFy9P51+kwL3B60l7QY5bZGMF0="`. Same on the real fixture: `hero-mountain.png`, 555376 bytes, hex `e66b552e6043510b…`, base64 `5mtVLmBDUQu1zUdAltGCCLHJdVVu8ajPxWXdY6AoNcE=` -> 200 in 13ms.
findings.fix: Add `uploadHeaders` to the begin response — a flat map of exactly the headers the signature covers, values already encoded server-side, e.g. `{"x-amz-checksum-sha256":"5mtVLmBD…","Content-Type":"image/png"}`. The client replays the map verbatim and never re-derives an encoding. Record it in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md as REQUIRED, beside DEC-47's ImageProvider item. Add a leg asserting the map's key set equals the URL's `X-Amz-SignedHeaders` minus `host`, so the two cannot drift.

findings.target: plan-v7 R2 work item 3 and PD-11; DEC-51 ("content-length SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping")
findings.finding: SigV4 signs an exact header VALUE, so a signed `Content-Length` pins the upload to exactly that many bytes and can never express a ceiling. The bucket therefore enforces `== byteSize`, never `<= MEDIA_MAX_BYTES`. The cap remains an API-side 422 taken BEFORE the mint — precisely what PD-11 dismisses as 'the API hoping'. The composition is still sound (refuse to mint above the cap, then pin the exact declared size) but R2's prose is not, and a worker who reads it literally and signs `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` produces a URL that accepts only a file of exactly the maximum size. Second, subtler cost: a size violation surfaces as `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, indistinguishable from a tampered URL, a wrong content-type or a broken signer — so the phone shows the same failure for a photo one byte off as for a misconfigured server.
findings.evidence: Signed `Content-Length: 29`; PUT 29000 bytes -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`, object absent. PUT exactly 29 bytes -> `200`. No chunked bypass: forcing `ContentLength = -1` (Transfer-Encoding: chunked) -> `411 MissingContentLength`, object absent. The only true range mechanism is a different upload shape: minio-go v7.3.0 `PostPolicy.SetContentLengthRange(1,1024)` returns err=nil and `PresignedPostPolicy` yields a URL plus 7 form fields.
findings.fix: Rewrite R2 item 3 to say what is actually enforced where: MEDIA_MAX_BYTES is an API-side refusal to MINT, and the signature pins the exact declared byteSize so a minted URL is not an unbounded write. Both sentences are needed; neither alone is true. If a genuine bucket-side range is wanted instead, say so and switch to presigned POST — that is a different client contract and a different step.

findings.target: plan-v7 R2 work item 6 and its acceptance_check (`docker compose up -d --wait  # three services healthy`); R4 `make seed`
findings.finding: Nothing in the plan creates the bucket. R2 adds MinIO as a compose service with a healthcheck and a named volume, and `media.Store` is PresignPut/PresignGet/Stat — no MakeBucket, no BucketExists. The official `quay.io/minio/minio` image auto-creates nothing. So R2's acceptance check passes (MinIO is healthy with zero buckets) and R4's `make seed` is the first thing that fails, three steps later, with an error that reads like a credentials problem.
findings.evidence: Fresh container, `ListBuckets` -> empty; `BucketExists("travellog-media")` -> false; `/minio/health/live` -> 200 the whole time. Presigning against a non-existent bucket fails at PRESIGN time, not at PUT: `PresignHeader("no-such-bucket-xyz", …)` -> err "The specified bucket does not exist".
findings.fix: In R2, at wiring time in cmd/api/main.go: `BucketExists` and `MakeBucket` if absent (idempotent, and it doubles as the reachability probe of the next finding). Or an `mc mb --ignore-existing` init service in compose with `depends_on: minio: service_healthy`. Either way name it in R2's work list and add it to the acceptance check — `up --wait` proving three healthy services is not proving the bucket exists.

findings.target: plan-v7 R3 work items 6 and 7; DEC-51's content-type allowlist; migrations/0003
findings.finding: DEC-51's allowlist is described as a defence in three layers and is actually two. The Go 422 and the 0003 CHECK both constrain the DATABASE ROW. Nothing constrains what the bucket stores or what a fetcher receives — the uploader sets `Content-Type` on the PUT and MinIO keeps it. So a row reading `image/png`, passing both enforcement points, can address an object the bucket serves as `text/html`.
findings.evidence: Presign covering only the checksum; PUT with `Content-Type: text/html` -> 200; `StatObject` -> `ct="text/html"`; presigned GET -> `Content-Type: text/html`. The disposition mitigation does hold — with `response-content-disposition=attachment` the response is `CD="attachment"` and cannot be stripped (removing the query param -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`) — but that is DEC-51's stated RESIDUAL, not the allowlist. The fix is measured working: adding `Content-Type: image/png` to the signed headers gives `SignedHeaders=content-type;host;x-amz-checksum-sha256`; sending `text/html` against it -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`; sending `image/png` -> `200` and `StatObject` -> `ct="image/png"`.
findings.fix: Sign Content-Type into the PUT alongside the checksum, sourced from the same validated value the 422 and the CHECK see. One header. It makes the allowlist reach the object rather than only the row, and it is the layer R3 item 7 believes it already has.

findings.target: internal/media/keys.go and the PresignPut call site (plan-v7 R2 work items 1-2)
findings.finding: The checksum binds the HEADER to the BODY. Nothing binds the header to the KEY — that is the mint site's job alone, and there is no leg for it. Measured: a PUT to key `<traveller>/<digestA>` carrying a self-consistent `x-amz-checksum-sha256` for entirely different bytes B succeeds with 200, and the address then holds bytes whose digest is not the address. Worse, versioning is off, so a second PUT at an already-committed key silently REPLACES the bytes. The whole content-addressing guarantee therefore rests on one unasserted line: that PresignPut derives the signed digest from the same variable the key derives from.
findings.evidence: P2-08: first PUT honest -> `PRESENT size=29 sha256="o+vra…"`; second PUT at the SAME key with lying bytes and a matching lying checksum -> `200`, `StatObject` now `size=45 etag=8ba0d244… sha256="2S2bk0BrYCIuCddv0bveyzstaEWo3oRlsMFlu4geG0w="`. The address no longer holds sha256(content). Closing it at the bucket is measured working: signing `If-None-Match: *` gives `SignedHeaders=host;if-none-match;x-amz-checksum-sha256`; first PUT -> 200; any second PUT -> `412 PreconditionFailed` with the original bytes intact, including the replacement attack above.
findings.fix: Two things, and they are not the same thing. (1) One function in keys.go returns the key AND the base64 header from one hex digest, so they cannot diverge; a mutation that computes them from two variables reddens a leg. (2) Sign `If-None-Match: *` so the bucket itself makes a content address write-once. Note the retry consequence for CLIENT-PREREQUISITES: a client re-PUTting after an unacknowledged success gets 412, which means 'already there', not 'failed' — commit must treat it as success.

findings.target: cmd/api/main.go (plan-v7 R2 work item 9, "panic on nil at wiring time"); R3 work item 5 ("presigning is a local HMAC")
findings.finding: Two claims that hold only after the first call. minio-go resolves the bucket region with a real network round trip on the first presign per bucket and caches it; before that cache is warm, presigning does I/O and can fail. So (a) a wrong `S3_SECRET_KEY` starts a perfectly healthy server whose every media route 500s — the wiring-time panic is on nil, not on reachability — and (b) `POST /v1/media/mint` for a twelve-photo grid is one blocking network call plus twelve local HMACs on a cold cache, with no timeout named anywhere.
findings.evidence: First presign on a fresh client: 9.864ms. Warm presigns: 16µs, 15µs, 13µs. Twelve presigned GETs warm: 161µs total. Wrong credentials -> err "The Access Key Id you provided does not exist in our records" at presign, and NOT cached — the second presign fails identically. MinIO down -> presign err `Get "http://…/lens-media/?location=": dial tcp: connect: connection refused`.
findings.fix: Do the BucketExists/MakeBucket call at startup (it is the previous finding's fix and it warms the location cache as a side effect, making R3's 'local HMAC' claim true from the first request). Then either add media to /healthz or state in the file that it is deliberately excluded and why — a healthy container that cannot mint a URL is the failure this catches.

findings.target: plan-v7 OE-12 (media.Store has no Remove); migrations/0001 media_objects_traveller_fk ON DELETE CASCADE
findings.finding: The orphan set is much narrower than the plan seems to fear, and completely unreclaimed. Measured, every partial or dishonest upload leaves NOTHING in the bucket — so there is exactly one orphan class from uploads: a SUCCESSFUL upload that is never committed, leaving `uploaded_at IS NULL` plus a real object, forever. `media.Store` has no Remove by decision, so no code path in R1-R8 can reclaim it and nothing bounds the bucket's size. There is a second, larger class the plan does not mention at all: `media_objects_traveller_fk ON DELETE CASCADE` drops every row when a traveller goes and leaves every object. Both are silent — no log line, no metric, no query.
findings.evidence: Partial upload (declare Content-Length 29 over a raw socket, send 10 bytes, close) -> object ABSENT. Zero-length body against a signed checksum -> `400 XAmzContentChecksumMismatch`, ABSENT. Checksum mismatch -> ABSENT. Oversized against a signed length -> ABSENT. Only the honest, uncommitted upload persists. Bucket default state: versioning `""` (disabled), `GetBucketLifecycle` -> "The lifecycle configuration does not exist", `GetBucketEncryption` -> "The server side encryption configuration was not found".
findings.fix: Do not add Remove — OE-12's reasoning stands. Do write the two classes down where a reader will find them, with the arithmetic: at fixture scale it is 1.0 MB and irrelevant; at 10,000 photographs it is not. A MinIO lifecycle rule expiring objects under a prefix after N days is the zero-code option and is worth naming as the deferred answer with its trigger, rather than leaving the reclaim question implicit in an interface that has no method for it.

findings.target: DEC-84 (S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC = 15m); plan-v7 R8 work item 8; the client's ui/log_image.dart
findings.finding: The 15-minute public window has no refresh path and no legible failure. R8 answers a JSON envelope with URLs embedded and `Cache-Control: no-store`; `POST /v1/media/mint` is authenticated, so an unauthenticated reader has no way to re-mint. Fifteen minutes is therefore a hard wall from the moment the envelope was generated, not a rolling window — whoever renders the share page must re-GET `/l/{token}` and nothing says so. On the phone the failure is worse than invisible: the client's `log_image.dart` draws a silent plate on any image error, and the client's own CLAUDE.md justifies that silence with "today every asset is bundled and declared, so a failure plate means a build defect rather than something a user can act on". A presigned URL makes that premise false — expiry is routine, user-actionable, and the plate says nothing.
findings.evidence: Expired presigned GET -> `403`, `Content-Type: application/xml`, `AccessDeniedRequest has expired`. Tampered signature -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`. Deleted object -> `404 NoSuchKey`. So the three are distinguishable on the wire, and none of them is distinguishable in the client's UI. `X-Amz-Expires=900` is a DELTA from `X-Amz-Date`, so config takes a duration and nothing needs a clock.
findings.fix: In R8, one sentence: the envelope's URLs are valid for S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC from generation and the renderer re-fetches `/l/{token}` to refresh them. In CLIENT-PREREQUISITES, add the expiry case to DEC-47's existing ImageProvider item — the same pass, since both are about the client learning that a picture can now fail for a reason a user can act on.

findings.target: plan-v7 R2 / DEC-38 — the two encodings
findings.finding: The hex-vs-base64 trap fails loudly and immediately, which is the good news, and the plan's own leg still cannot see it, which is the bad news. A worker who signs the hex string is refused on 100% of uploads including honest ones, with an error code distinct from a real mismatch. But the leg the step exists for asserts only `resp.StatusCode < 400`, and the hex mistake returns 400 — so it is green.
findings.evidence: Honest bytes, HEX digest in `x-amz-checksum-sha256` -> `400 InvalidArgument`, message "Invalid checksum provided.", object absent. Contrast a genuine mismatch: `400 XAmzContentChecksumMismatch`. The schema already pins the other half correctly — `media_objects_id_sha256_ck CHECK (id ~ '^[0-9a-f]{64}$')` — so base64 exists nowhere but inside the signer and the `uploadHeaders` map.
findings.fix: Same as the first blocker: assert the error code. `InvalidArgument` and `XAmzContentChecksumMismatch` are different sentences and only one of them is the control passing.

findings.target: plan-v7 R3 work item 7 — "V4-SF3's correct removal of nosniff, which S3's closed response-header override set cannot produce"
findings.finding: Correct about S3 and a live trap for anyone who writes a leg about it. MinIO sets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on presigned GETs of its own accord. So a test asserting the mitigation is present would pass locally by measuring MinIO's default and would silently stop being true in production — DEC-43's 'MinIO is a more forgiving verifier' hazard running in the opposite direction, where the local server is more generous than the real one.
findings.evidence: Every presigned GET in this run returned `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, including on an object stored as `text/html`, both with and without the disposition override.
findings.fix: Keep V4-SF3's comment and add the measurement to it, so it is not re-litigated by someone who curls MinIO and sees the header. Do not write a leg asserting nosniff.

findings.target: plan-v7 R8 — the public envelope's size and the nature of the URL it embeds
findings.finding: Two numbers worth having before R8's envelope is quoted, and one sentence about what the URL is. A presigned URL is 394 characters, so twelve in one envelope is ~4.7 kB of JSON on top of R4's measured 85,422-byte read. And the URL is a pure bearer capability: unlimited replay, and unsigned request headers such as Range are accepted.
findings.evidence: URL length 394 chars at `X-Amz-Expires=900`. Three replays of one URL -> 200, 200, 200. Unsigned `Range: bytes=0-4` -> `206`. `DELETE` against a GET-signed URL -> `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch` (the method is covered). Swapping the traveller UUID segment in a minted URL -> `403` (the path is covered).
findings.fix: One sentence in R8: each URL in the envelope is a bearer capability with no replay limit, which is what makes `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` load-bearing rather than hygiene — it is what keeps the capability out of the next site's logs.

findings.finding: The plan discusses a database backup and never a media backup. Restoring the database alone gives a log whose 308 media references all resolve — `cities_cover_fk` and its siblings are satisfied by rows in `media_objects`, which come back with the dump — pointing at bytes that are gone. The failure is not an error anywhere; it is 308 broken images and a foreign-key graph that looks perfectly healthy.
findings.evidence: Bucket default state measured: versioning disabled, no lifecycle, no encryption configuration. `media_objects` rows are ordinary table rows and travel with any dump; the objects do not.
findings.fix: Name it in deferred_decisions with a trigger, alongside bucket creation, lifecycle and encryption-at-rest — all four are absent from R1-R8 and only the first is needed now. The honest sentence is that a database restore without a bucket restore is a silently broken log.

verified_correct: THE LOAD-BEARING ASSUMPTION HOLDS. MinIO enforces `x-amz-checksum-sha256` and refuses mismatched bytes. Measured on RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z (commit 07c3a429), arm64: PresignHeader-signed PUT + lying bytes, header correctly replayed -> `400 XAmzContentChecksumMismatch` ("The provided 'x-amz-checksum' header does not match what was computed") and the object is ABSENT afterwards, confirmed by an admin-credential StatObject rather than by a HEAD. At real size: one bit flipped in the middle of hero-mountain.png (555,376 bytes) -> the same refusal, nothing stored. The plan's `[assumed]` marker can come off.

THE BAN IS EARNED, AND THE FAIL-OPEN IS REAL. `PresignedPutObject` produces `X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host` only; a PUT of entirely different bytes to a key naming sha256(X) returns `200` and the object is stored at the poisoned address. Confirmed in source that PresignHeader is the only one of the three that signs extra headers: `Presign` calls `presignURL(..., nil)` (api-presigned.go:111-113).

A SECOND, FREE CONTROL THE PLAN DOES NOT USE. The stored checksum is readable at commit time: `StatObject` with `StatObjectOptions{Checksum: true}` returns `ChecksumSHA256` in base64, and base64-decoding it to hex equals the object id exactly (verified on both fixture PNGs). Two consequences — R3's commit HEAD can verify the DIGEST as well as the size at no extra call, and an object uploaded through the banned `PresignedPutObject` path has `ChecksumSHA256 == ""`, so requiring a non-empty matching value at commit is a RUNTIME guard against the ban rather than a grep. Note the flag: without `Checksum: true` the field comes back empty and the check would silently pass nothing.

hex on the wire / base64 in the header is correct and necessary, not a stylistic split. MinIO refuses hex in the header with `InvalidArgument`, and `media_objects_id_sha256_ck` pins the id to hex, so base64 exists only inside the signer.
`<traveller_uuid>/<sha256>` is safe against cross-traveller reach: the signature covers the path, and swapping the traveller segment of a minted URL gives `403`.

`response-content-disposition=attachment` works on a presigned GET and is SIGNED, so the URL holder cannot strip it — deleting the query parameter gives `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`. Measured `Content-Disposition: attachment` on the response.

Content-Length signing genuinely binds and has no chunked bypass: forcing Transfer-Encoding chunked against a length-signed URL gives `411 MissingContentLength` and stores nothing. (See the blocker above for what it binds — exact, not maximum.)

Checksum and Content-Length can be signed together without interfering: `SignedHeaders=content-length;host;x-amz-checksum-sha256`, honest -> 200, oversized -> 403, and the two reddens are independent, which is the pair R2 wants for its 'two controls rather than one' argument.

TTL bounds are inside minio-go's limits with room: `< 1s` -> "Expires cannot be lesser than 1 second"; `7d` -> ok; `7d + 1s` -> "Expires cannot be greater than 7 days". 2m and 15m both fine. `X-Amz-Expires` is a delta from `X-Amz-Date`, so config takes a duration and no clock is involved.

THE FIXTURE'S TWO DIGESTS, CONFIRMED AGAINST THE ACTUAL BYTES. `internal/logbook/testdata/client_sample_log.json` holds 284 photographs across exactly 2 assets — `card-ireland.png` 189, `hero-mountain.png` 95 — plus 6 trip, 9 city and 9 place covers: 308 references, 2 objects, 1,084,768 bytes. Both digests match DEC-77's recorded prefixes (e66b552e6043510b…, 8dfb203bc0f89065…). Seed uploads measured at 13ms and 19ms.
DEC-42's config seam is right for the reason given: the signature covers `host`, so the public address cannot be a constant.

Nothing I ran touched the live stack. My MinIO ran on 127.0.0.1:9412/9413 in its own container and named volume, both destroyed; `travellog-api-1` and `travellog-postgres-1` were untouched throughout.
questions_for_human: Should Content-Type be signed into the PUT? It is measured working and it is what makes DEC-51's allowlist reach the object rather than only the row. It costs one more header the client must replay exactly, and it makes a content-type mismatch a 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch rather than a 422 — a worse error for a legitimate client that guesses its own MIME type wrong.

Should `If-None-Match: *` be signed into the PUT, making a content address write-once at the bucket? Measured working on MinIO (first PUT 200, any second 412 PreconditionFailed, original bytes intact). The consequence to accept is the retry story: a client re-uploading after an unacknowledged success gets 412, which means 'already there' and must be treated as success by the commit path, not as a failure.

The 95/189 asset split is EXACTLY the same partition as R4's measured '95 have both placeId and visitId, 189 have neither'. That is a fixture coincidence, and it means a test that confuses 'which asset' with 'which coherence class' cannot tell them apart — including R4's own stated mutation, 'point one locator at the other's digest', whose 189-row diff is numerically identical to the coherence split. Worth breaking in the fixture, or worth a comment?

Who bounds the bucket, and when? Nothing in R1-R8 reclaims an object, `Remove` is deliberately absent (OE-12), there is no lifecycle rule, and `ON DELETE CASCADE` on the traveller silently orphans everything. At the fixture's 1.0 MB this is nothing; the question is whether the deferral gets a trigger now or is discovered later.

Revocation of an ALREADY-MINTED URL has exactly two levers — delete the object (measured: the same unexpired URL immediately returns 404 NoSuchKey) or rotate the S3 secret (reasoned, not executed). Neither is reachable from the code the plan describes. Is DEC-84's 'up to fifteen minutes' honest sentence the whole intended answer, or is one of those levers meant to exist?
unverifiable: Everything here is MinIO RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z, not AWS S3. The asymmetry matters and cuts in the project's favour for the finding that counts: DEC-43's premise is that MinIO is the MORE FORGIVING verifier, so a REFUSAL measured here is strong evidence (a stricter server also refuses) while an ACCEPTANCE is weak. The one acceptance that is load-bearing — PresignedPutObject plus lying bytes returning 200 — is safe in the other direction too, since S3 has no digest to check when none is signed. But it was not measured against S3.

Whether AWS S3 refuses a chunked PUT the same way MinIO does (411 MissingContentLength). S3 supports `aws-chunked` with `x-amz-decoded-content-length`, which would be an unsigned x-amz header here and therefore refused — reasoned, not measured.
Whether rotating the S3 secret invalidates outstanding presigned URLs. It follows from SigV4 deriving the signing key from the secret, but I did not rotate the running container's root credentials.
Whether S3 or MinIO honours `If-None-Match: *` identically. Measured on MinIO only; S3 gained conditional writes in November 2024 and behaves the same by documentation, not by measurement here.

IAM/STS behaviour. These probes used static root credentials, so every URL lived its full TTL. Under temporary credentials a presigned URL dies with the session, which would cap both TTLs at something shorter than configured — relevant only if the deployment ever moves off static keys.
Real-S3 bucket policies, server-side encryption behaviour, and anything about cost or request-rate limits at scale.
